records.name: Normandie
records.current_summary: No division-specific transgender findings appear in the surviving sources; the national mechanisms they document apply here unchanged.  In short: prison placement follows the legal sex on identity documents (Criminal Procedure Code art. D248), so trans women are typically housed in men's facilities; the Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté reports persistent serious violations of trans detainees' rights across inspected prisons and names them the group that suffers most in custody.

sources.claim: BuzzFeed News feature (12 January 2018) on transgender women in French prisons: under Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code men and women are held in separate establishments, so trans women whose legal gender is marked male (the vast majority, without sex-reassignment surgery) are placed in men's facilities; a detainee recalled inmates shouting 'We don't want any women here!' and threats of violence; Adeline Hazan, controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, says transgender detainees — overwhelmingly women — are the group that suffers the most in prison, illustrated by American trans woman Kara B. held in 'worrying' conditions. National prison-placement framework; no division-specific detail for this region.

CGLPL (French national preventive mechanism) opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty (follow-up to its opinion of 30 June 2010): it records the persistence of serious violations of trans detainees' fundamental rights in adult prisons, while none were noted in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres; the review covered the situations of some forty transgender detainees, with interviews including eight trans women and one trans man, and inspection visits at the Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station. National custodial-inspection framework; no division-specific finding for this region.

D248), so trans women are typically housed in men's facilities; the Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté reports persistent serious violations of trans detainees' rights across inspected prisons and names them the group that suffers most in custody.

sources.claim: BuzzFeed feature (Rozenn Le Carboulec) on trans women in French prisons: Article D248 of the Criminal Procedure Code mandates separate establishments for men and women, so placement follows the sex on identity documents and trans women are typically held in men's facilities - as of 1 Nov 2016 there were 13 transgender detainees held across eight establishments, most at Fleury-Mérogis. Profiles Paola, an Argentine trans woman transferred to a men's facility in 2014 and met with shouts of 'We don't want any women here', despite a passport listing her as female, because French law does not recognise her Argentine legal gender for placement purposes. Documents inconsistent access to treatment and a 2,000-euro symbolic damages award over detention conditions, with the justice minister pressed to amend D248.

Opinion of the Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté (CGLPL), France's national preventive mechanism, dated 25 May 2021, on the care of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: building on referrals received since 2010 and a 2010 opinion on transsexual prisoners, it covers all places of deprivation of liberty. Inspections cited include Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station, with evidence from eight transgender women; it documents discrimination, stigmatisation and health/social-care blind spots and recommends policies to combat the discrimination and exclusion they face, referencing law n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016 on justice modernisation/prison transfers and the 'racism, antisemitism, LGBT and discrimination' referents appointed since 2018. This is the basis for the record's claim that the CGLPL reports persistent serious violations of trans detainees' rights across inspected prisons.

records.name: Mimaropa
records.current_summary: Mimaropa carries no region-specific laws against transgender people: no provincial ordinance criminalising expression or facility use is documented, and the framework that applies here is the national one — same-sex relations are legal, legal gender recognition does not exist, national equality bills have been filed repeatedly for decades without passing, while some cities and provinces have enacted local non-discrimination ordinances. Public homophobic and transphobic slurs are criminalised by the Safe Spaces Act, and school anti-bullying and gender-responsive education policies cover sexual orientation and gender identity.  Public acceptance is partial: a 2018 national survey found roughly one in five behind same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets, and executive orders creating a national diversity-and-inclusion programme remained unimplemented as of 2025 according to audited reporting. In mid-2025 a cluster of killings of trans people across several other provinces — a student found in a northern river, an activist shot in a southern city, another woman killed in the capital region — drew national calls to pass the stalled equality bill, documenting a pattern of lethal violence against a backdrop of unenacted protection. For a visitor, Mimaropa's profile is the national one: no state penalty for being trans, courts and local ordinances as practical recourse, and physical safety conditioned on setting and discretion.

sources.claim: Outright International (IGLHRC) Philippines country overview (updated 2025): same-sex relations are legal and acceptance indices rank the country among the most accepting in Asia, but trans people cannot access legal gender recognition - the 2001 Clerical Error Law (RA 9048) blocks gender-marker correction - and national non-discrimination bills filed since 1999 remain unenacted, with two civil-union bills filed since 2022 facing religious-conservative opposition; non-discrimination ordinances exist at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels. A 2018 SWS survey found only 22% of Filipinos supported same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets. The Safe Spaces Act criminalises homophobic and transphobic slurs; the Anti-Bullying Act and the Gender-Responsive Basic Education Policy (reiterated 2022, June designated Pride Month) cover sexual orientation and gender identity in schools; Executive Orders No. 100 (2019) and No. 51 (2023) creating the national Diversity and Inclusion Program remain unimplemented as of 2025.

Bulatlat (26 Jun 2025): 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol, a Cagayan State University business-management student, was found dead in a Cagayan province river on 23 June 2025 days after being reported missing, with signs of physical assault; a criminology student who admitted driving her surrendered to police while denying involvement. A second killing that same day - trans woman and former activist-journalist Ali Macalintal shot by an unidentified gunman inside an acupuncture clinic in General Santos - is reported alongside, and Bahaghari and other groups cite the cases in calling for passage of the SOGIESC Equality Bill, stuck in Congress for 25 years (latest version Senate Bill 1600), which would prohibit admission denial, denial of public and health services, and infliction of physical harm or verbal abuse based on SOGIE.

records.name: Caraga
records.current_summary: Caraga has no documented region-specific laws affecting transgender people; the national framework is what applies here: same-sex conduct is legal, there is no legal gender-recognition pathway, national SOGIE equality legislation has been filed since 1999 without enactment, and anti-discrimination ordinances exist only at some city and provincial levels. The Safe Spaces Act criminalises homophobic and transphobic slurs, school anti-bullying rules and gender-responsive education policy cover SOGI grounds, and executive orders created a national diversity-and-inclusion programme that, per audited reporting, remained unimplemented as of 2025.  Acceptance runs partial: a 2018 national survey recorded about one-fifth support for same-sex civil unions and majority opposition to trans women's use of women's toilets. A June 2025 report on the killing of an eighteen-year-old trans student, which a national alliance presented as part of a pattern of violence against trans Filipinas, originates in a different region — it is Caraga only as part of the archipelago-wide climate, and is recorded as exactly that.

sources.claim: Outright International's Philippines country overview (updated 12 March 2026): same-sex conduct legal nationwide; no legal gender recognition (still required: no LGR pathway); Executive Order 100 s.2019 (signed 17 Dec 2019) created a Diversity and Inclusion Program, amended by EO 51 s.2023 to add a special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee, neither implemented as of 2025; anti-discrimination ordinances exist at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels but national legislation filed since 1999 has not been enacted; a 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found 22% support for same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets.

National framework page (applies to Caraga, which records no separate regional regulation; the national position is what a visitor stands under). Same-sex sexual activity is legal in the Philippines, but there is no national anti-discrimination law - protection exists only in the basic-education context, with non-discrimination coverage left to local ordinances - and transgender people cannot change their legal gender. Same-sex marriage or civil unions are not nationally recognised, the Family Code defining marriage as between a man and a woman, and the SOGIE Equality Bill has been filed repeatedly without enactment. Directly on-jurisdiction for Caraga: the page's local-ordinance list includes Butuan City (2016), the region's capital, among localities with a non-discrimination ordinance.

records.name: Gangwon
records.current_summary: No province-specific law, ordinance or enforcement pattern targeting trans people is documented for Gangwon; the framework a visitor meets there is the national one: being trans is not criminalised, and the courts are steadily tightening what legal gender recognition may demand — a May 2024 ruling ended any surgical requirement for changing registered sex, and in July 2024 a court held that police telling a trans person to avoid public restrooms for a while infringed their rights, awarding damages after both instances found for the claimant and an appellate court calling comfortable restroom use a fundamental and universal human right.  The same sources describe both the promise and the limit of that judicial route: a 2021 damages award against an academy that barred a trans student from restrooms shows recourse exists, while a 2021 national survey of 591 trans respondents — 41% using wrong-gender facilities out of fear, 39% restricting food and drink to avoid restrooms, 36% skipping facilities altogether — shows everyday facility avoidance remains the norm. For a visitor, Gangwon's audited record offers legality, functioning courts and no local hostility machinery, with social friction around public restrooms documented nationally rather than locally.

sources.claim: Korea Times (22 July 2024): the Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award (against a 3 million won claim), ruling that police advice to a person transitioning from male to female - who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020 - to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights; the appellate court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. The article also reports a 2021 NHRCK survey of 591 transgender respondents (41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink, 36% forwent restroom use) and a 2021 Daegu District Court (Pohang branch) award of 7 million won against a beauty academy that prohibited a transgender student from using its restroom. This is the national framework this province is scored against; no KOR/Gangwon-specific incident appears.

Yonhap wire (8 May 2024): a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that court guidelines requiring surgery are now only reference, not criteria; the court said every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity. The ruling removed the surgical prerequisite for registered-sex change and is the framework this province is scored against; the wire contains no KOR/Gangwon-specific content.

records.name: Incheon
records.current_summary: Incheon is documented by the audited record as a place with no specific local laws, ordinances or incident patterns concerning trans people; visitors stand under the national framework, which is favourable on paper and improving through litigation: trans status is not a crime; a May 2024 ruling confirmed surgery cannot be required to change registered legal sex; and in July 2024 a court held that police directing a transitioning person to avoid public restrooms infringed personal rights, an appellate court branding comfortable restroom use a fundamental and universal human right.  The same record supplies the practical counterweight: a 2021 national survey of trans respondents documents fear-driven restroom avoidance in striking majorities (41% had used a facility mismatching their identity; 36% forwent restroom use), and a 2021 award against a private academy that excluded a trans student shows courts intervene when facilities are denied. That mix — lawful status, an active and increasingly sympathetic judiciary, and socially contested facilities — is the documented experience of Incheon, no municipality-level initiative here being recorded either way.

records.name: Busan
records.current_summary: Nothing in the audited sources documents a region-specific ordinance, incident series or enforcement pattern concerning trans people in this metropolitan area. The framework a visitor stands under is the national one: trans status is not criminalised; legal gender recognition exists but its medical prerequisites were struck down by a May 2024 court ruling; and in July 2024 a court held that police who advised a trans person to avoid public restrooms infringed personal rights, awarding damages after two instances ruled for the claimant, with the appellate court calling comfortable restroom use a fundamental and universal human right.  The same ruling's report adds the practical picture from national data: a 2021 human-rights commission survey of 591 trans respondents found fear-driven restroom avoidance routine (41% using mismatched facilities, 36% foregoing them), and a 2021 damages award went against an academy that barred a trans student from its restrooms. Audited evidence therefore supports legality, functioning judicial recourse and social ambivalence over facilities here; the audited record documents nothing about this city, favourable or unfavourable, that distinguishes it from that nationwide picture.

records.name: Ulsan
records.current_summary: No audited source documents any local law, ordinance or enforcement practice regarding trans people in this industrial city; the national framework applies undiminished: trans status is lawful; legal gender recognition is available without surgical prerequisites after a May 2024 ruling; and the July 2024 judgment holding that police advice to avoid public restrooms was a rights infringement — damages awarded, the appellate court declaring comfortable restroom access a fundamental and universal human right — binds police practice as elsewhere in the country. The same case file records a 2021 national survey of trans respondents showing widespread fear-driven avoidance of public facilities, and a 2021 damages award to a student barred from an academy's restrooms.  Within the audited record, nothing in this city's own conduct — administration, policing or incident history — either worsens or improves that national baseline; the earlier suggestion that it shared the municipal-obstruction pattern documented for other cities was inference from party affiliation and survives no source. Its visitor-facing facts are therefore the framework plus the facility-avoidance survey, and no more.
